dTIP7g9j8r8.title: Live Portfolio Review: Your Hero Section Is Costing You The Interview
dTIP7g9j8r8.description: Tyler and Nick roast real, anonymized product design portfolio hero sections and show how to rewrite generic hero copy into a clear, specific positioning line.
takeaways: Generic hero copy tells a recruiter nothing. Say what you do and who you do it for.
Run the dream job exercise: write the hero for the one job you want, then cut everything that doesn't serve it.
Expert in X beats curious about X. Pick the niche and own it.

q6zoDGZ0Pgo.title: Product Design Money Talk: How To Go From $50 To $95 An Hour Doing The Same Work
q6zoDGZ0Pgo.description: Tyler and Nick talk salaries, raises and freelance rates, including the three times revenue framework for asking for a raise with numbers.
takeaways: Ask for a raise with the three times revenue framework. Show what you bring in against what you cost.
Benchmark the band before you apply, and negotiate while you still have a job.
Freelancing? Raise your rate with every new client until the rejections start. That's your ceiling.

lLkZCxNWHMY.title: How a Product Design Director Uses AI to Explore 10 Ideas At Once
lLkZCxNWHMY.description: Tyler walks through his full AI prototyping process: ten directions in one clickable prototype, flow mapping first, and checking ideas against the real codebase.
takeaways: Ask Claude for ten directions in one prototype with a toggle, then narrow with engineering and product in the room.
Map the flow and edge cases in FigJam before you prompt anything.
Check ideas against the real app with a GitHub connector so you only scope what fits.

lWOCng5xmeE.title: I Spent a Month Trying to Quit Figma. It Failed.
lWOCng5xmeE.description: Tyler and Nick on vibe coding, designers touching code, and why polished product design still needs taste and craft that AI tools miss.
takeaways: A month of trying to skip Figma fell apart on polish. Spacing, type and the small pixel calls AI still misses.
Filter new tools by your own workflow, never by the latest demo.
Transcripts as context are the boring AI unlock that actually saves time.

1zJGFE2hFS8.title: The 4 Real Reasons Companies Hire Designers (And How to Prove Your Value), Part 1
1zJGFE2hFS8.description: The business reasons companies hire designers, and how to connect UX work to revenue, conversion, adoption and cost reduction in your case studies.
takeaways: Companies hire designers to make money or save money. Frame every metric as one of the two.
Make money: conversion, MRR, adoption. Save money: support costs and operational waste.
No access to metrics? Benchmark your impact and say what you would have measured.

jMFZon1zh4w.title: (Live) Senior Product Designers Solve a Real User Adoption Problem
jMFZon1zh4w.description: A live working session where Tyler and Nick tackle low feature adoption and weak upgrade conversion, from awareness and email sequencing to pricing tiers.
takeaways: Watch a real working session on one problem: low feature adoption and weak upgrades.
Score your adoption levers before picking a fix. Awareness, in-app nudges, email, pricing tiers.
Product blames awareness, design blames UX, marketing blames messaging. The session gets them on the same problem.

DrCn7wQe2Rw.title: Your Stakeholders Don't Care About UX. Now What?!
DrCn7wQe2Rw.description: Tyler and Nick on stakeholders who want to skip research and just ship, why designers work like an insurance policy, and how to reframe design in the language executives respond to.
takeaways: Your job works like an insurance policy between an idea and production. Say it that way.
Reframe research as risk reduction. That's language executives already respond to.
Sell design through the company's goals and KPIs, and stop apologizing for your process.

wp1pifLvVyY.title: The 4 Real Reasons Companies Hire Designers (And How to Prove Your Value), Part 2
wp1pifLvVyY.description: Part 2: the overlooked reasons designers get hired, from time savings and operational efficiency to risk reduction and compliance, with real examples from construction and pharma.
takeaways: Time saved is impact. Translate the hours into money and it lands in any case study.
Risk reduction counts too. Compliance issues, errors and lawsuits that never happened.
Real examples from construction workflows and pharma packaging show impact well past the visuals.
